question: Do I need a fractional CRO for my proptech company?
body:
## Direct Answer

For most proptech companies between roughly 1 and 15 million dollars in annual recurring revenue, a fractional CRO is the right call when go-to-market is your bottleneck but you cannot yet justify a 300k plus base salary plus equity for a full-time executive. Hire one when you have product-market fit signals and a founder-led sales ceiling, not when you are still hunting for your first repeatable deal. Skip it if your revenue problem is really a product or pricing problem in disguise.

Proptech founders sit in an awkward middle. The sales motion is genuinely complex — long procurement cycles, multiple stakeholders across owners, operators, brokers, and tenants, and buyers who are famously slow to adopt technology — yet the company is often too early to absorb a seven-figure fully-loaded revenue leader. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is designed for exactly this gap: senior GTM leadership for two to four days a week, on a monthly retainer instead of a full comp package. Below we walk through when it fits, what it costs, what it should actually deliver, and how to tell the difference between a revenue leadership gap and a problem no CRO can fix.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a proptech company?

A fractional CRO is a part-time revenue executive who owns the entire top-line engine: sales, marketing alignment, revenue operations, pricing, and forecasting. Unlike a consultant who diagnoses and hands you a deck, a fractional CRO operates. They sit in your pipeline reviews, they coach your account executives, they sign off on comp plans, and they carry a number. The distinction matters because proptech GTM problems are rarely solved by a strategy document — they are solved by someone rebuilding the motion week over week while deals are live.

In a proptech context specifically, the role skews toward a few concrete jobs. First, translating a horizontal technology story into vertical value that a regional property manager or a REIT asset team actually cares about — occupancy, NOI, tenant retention, maintenance cost, leasing velocity. Second, building a multi-threaded enterprise motion, because proptech deals almost never close on a single champion; you need the operations lead, the finance approver, and often an on-site property team all nodding. Third, standing up the revenue operations spine — CRM hygiene, stage definitions, and a forecast the board can trust. A good fractional leader treats [pipeline architecture](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11133) as the first deliverable, not an afterthought, because everything downstream depends on it.

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my proptech company — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9259-b1.jpg)


It helps to be concrete about what the first ninety days actually look like, because "owns the revenue engine" is abstract until you watch someone do it. Week one is usually a listening and data audit: the fractional leader pulls every closed-won and closed-lost deal from the last four quarters, interviews the founder and any existing reps, and sits in on two or three live calls without intervening. By week three they have a written diagnosis — which segment converts, where deals actually die, and which parts of the current "process" are folklore rather than fact. By week six they are rewriting the qualification criteria and the discovery script, and by the end of the first quarter they have either validated or killed at least one assumption the founder held sacred. That sequence — audit, diagnose, rebuild, then scale — is what separates an operator from an advisor, and it is worth asking a candidate to walk you through their version of it before you sign anything.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Founder led sales ceiling] --> B[Fractional CRO engages]
    B --> C[Fix ICP and messaging]
    B --> D[Build repeatable playbook]
    B --> E[Stand up RevOps and forecast]
    C --> F[Multi threaded proptech deals]
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G[Predictable pipeline]
    G --> H[Hire full time CRO or VP Sales]

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my proptech company — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9259-b2.jpg)

```

The end state of a healthy engagement is that the fractional leader works themselves out of a job. They install the system, hire or level up the first real sales leaders, and hand off to a full-time executive once revenue can fund one. If a fractional CRO is still indispensable to closing deals after eighteen months, the engagement has quietly failed at its actual purpose. The best fractional CROs are almost eager to make themselves redundant, because a clean, documented handoff is the reference story that wins them their next client. Be wary of anyone whose incentives quietly favor staying forever — the model only works when the goal is a durable internal capability, not a permanent external dependency.

## When should a proptech founder hire a fractional CRO versus a VP of Sales?

The cleanest test is whether you need a builder or a doer. A VP of Sales is a doer-leader: they take an existing, largely-working motion and scale it by hiring reps, enforcing process, and hitting a quota. A fractional CRO is a builder: they figure out what the motion should even be when it is still ambiguous. Proptech companies frequently mis-order these two hires — they bring in an expensive VP of Sales to scale a motion that does not yet exist, the VP flails because there is no playbook to execute, and eighteen months of runway evaporates.

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my proptech company — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9259-b3.jpg)


Hire the fractional CRO first when any of these are true: your founder is still the best (or only) closer; your pipeline forecast is a guess; your win rate swings wildly deal to deal; or you genuinely do not know which of three proptech buyer segments is your real ICP. Hire the VP of Sales instead when you already have two or three reps consistently hitting quota against a documented playbook and you simply need someone to run and expand that team. The fractional CRO builds the machine; the VP runs it. In the messy middle where proptech usually lives, the machine does not exist yet, which is precisely why fractional revenue leadership tends to fit better than a premature full-time hire.

There is also a capital-efficiency argument. A full-time CRO in proptech commands a base in the 250k to 350k range plus variable and meaningful equity — call it 400k plus fully loaded. If your ARR is under about 5 million, that single hire can be 8 to 15 percent of your entire revenue, and if you get the hire wrong, the recovery cost includes lost quarters, not just severance. A fractional engagement caps that downside dramatically while still buying you senior judgment.

The sequencing matters more than founders usually appreciate, because the two hires build on each other. The ideal path is often a fractional CRO who spends nine to twelve months constructing the motion and the RevOps spine, then leads the search for — and helps interview — the full-time VP of Sales who will inherit it. That way the VP walks into a documented playbook, a clean CRM, and a forecast that already works, instead of into ambiguity. Founders who skip the fractional step and hire the VP directly are effectively asking a scaler to also be an inventor, and those are genuinely different skill sets that rarely live in the same person. When you interview VP candidates, notice whether they light up at "here is a working machine, go make it bigger" or at "figure out what our machine should be" — the honest ones will tell you which problem they are actually good at.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost, and what is the ROI math?

Fractional CRO pricing generally runs as a monthly retainer tied to days of commitment. Typical market ranges land somewhere between 8,000 and 25,000 dollars per month depending on seniority, days per week, and whether equity is part of the package — a two-day-a-week engagement sits near the bottom, a near-full-time four-day arrangement with a proven operator near the top. Many engagements also carry a modest equity or success component so incentives align with revenue outcomes rather than billable hours. Always confirm current figures directly with candidates and your own market, since compensation moves and varies by region; treat any single number here as illustrative, not a quote.

The ROI question is not "is this cheaper than a full-time CRO" — it is "does the revenue lift exceed the retainer." Frame it against the cost of the alternative: a mis-hired full-time executive, or a founder spending 60 percent of their week on sales they are not equipped to systematize. If a 12,000-a-month engagement converts a stalled 800k pipeline into 300k of closed ARR over two quarters that would not have closed otherwise, the retainer is rounding error. The failure mode is not overpaying for the retainer — it is hiring a fractional leader to fix a problem that better [pricing and packaging](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11340) or a product gap actually caused.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Monthly retainer 8k to 25k] --> B{Revenue lift greater than cost}
    B -->|Yes| C[Keep and scale engagement]
    B -->|No| D[Diagnose root cause]
    D --> E[Product gap]
    D --> F[Pricing problem]
    D --> G[Wrong ICP]
    E --> H[Not a CRO fix]
    F --> H
    G --> C
```

A disciplined founder sets a 90-day and a 180-day scorecard before signing: pipeline created, stage conversion, forecast accuracy, and at least one leading indicator like qualified meetings from the new ICP. If those numbers do not move by the second quarter, the engagement is either mis-scoped or the revenue problem was never a leadership problem.

It is also worth modeling the hidden costs on both sides of the ledger so the comparison is honest. A full-time CRO carries recruiting fees, a ramp period of one to two quarters before they contribute, benefits, and the severance-plus-lost-momentum tax if it does not work out — a mis-hire at that level routinely costs a proptech company well over half a million dollars once you count the wasted runway. A fractional engagement, by contrast, ramps in weeks rather than quarters because the whole point is senior pattern recognition applied fast, and the exit cost is a thirty-day notice rather than a negotiated package. When you put those risk-adjusted numbers side by side, the fractional model often wins not because the monthly rate is lower but because the variance is lower. For a company with limited runway, reducing the blast radius of a wrong decision can matter more than optimizing the average case.

## What proptech-specific challenges should a fractional CRO be able to handle?

Proptech is not generic B2B SaaS, and a fractional CRO who has only sold horizontal software will struggle. The first specific challenge is the buyer's structural slowness. Real estate operators run on thin technology budgets, long depreciation mindsets, and a "we have always done it this way" culture. Deals that a horizontal SaaS rep expects to close in 60 days routinely take 6 to 9 months because the buyer is coordinating across on-site property staff, regional operations, and corporate finance. A capable fractional leader designs the motion around that reality — sequenced multi-stakeholder plays, pilot-to-rollout land-and-expand structures, and ROI cases denominated in the metrics real estate people actually manage to.

The second challenge is proving value in the buyer's own language. Occupancy, net operating income, leasing velocity, resident retention, and maintenance cost per unit are the currencies of the industry. A fractional CRO worth their retainer will rebuild your sales narrative around those numbers rather than around software features. The third is channel complexity: much of proptech distribution runs through property management companies, brokerages, MLS relationships, and integration partners, so partnership and channel strategy is often as important as direct sales. Founders should probe a candidate's actual real-estate-adjacent track record hard — the domain gap is the single most common reason a generalist fractional CRO underdelivers in this vertical. Cross-reference their approach with how you already think about your [ideal customer profile](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11208) before you sign.

A fourth challenge, easy to overlook, is the pilot trap. Real estate buyers love pilots because a single-property or single-portfolio trial fits their risk-averse, prove-it-first culture — but pilots are where proptech revenue goes to die if the motion is not designed to convert them. A weak operator lets a pilot drift for months with no defined success criteria, no executive sponsor on the buyer side, and no contractual path to rollout, and then acts surprised when the champion changes jobs and the deal evaporates. A strong fractional CRO structures every pilot as a time-boxed experiment with pre-agreed metrics, a named economic buyer who has committed to a rollout decision if the metrics hit, and a rollout price already on the table. That discipline — turning the buyer's instinct to test into a mechanism that actually closes — is one of the highest-leverage things a proptech-literate revenue leader brings, and it is nearly invisible on a résumé, so you have to ask about it directly.

## How should a proptech founder structure and onboard a fractional CRO engagement?

Structure determines outcome more than the individual's résumé does, so treat the engagement design as its own decision. Start with scope: write down, before you interview anyone, the three or four outcomes you actually need in the next two quarters — a validated ICP, a documented playbook, a trustworthy forecast, a first sales hire. A fractional CRO can do all of these eventually, but committing them to a sequence forces both sides to agree on what "done" looks like each month rather than letting the retainer become an open-ended relationship. Vague scope is the single most common reason these engagements feel expensive: not because the rate was wrong, but because nobody defined the deliverable.

Onboarding should be fast and access-heavy. Give the fractional leader real authority in week one — CRM admin rights, a seat in every pipeline review, direct access to the founder's calendar for the first month, and explicit air cover to change things that are not working. The failure pattern is hiring a senior operator and then treating them like an advisor who needs permission for every move; that wastes both the money and the expertise. Equally important is deciding, up front, who owns which decisions: comp plan changes, hiring and firing of reps, pricing exceptions, and forecast calls. A clean RACI on those four items prevents most of the friction that stalls fractional engagements around month three. Finally, agree on the handoff trigger from day one — the revenue level, the team size, or the calendar date at which you will bring the motion in-house — so that the engagement has a defined finish line and the fractional leader is building toward transferring the system rather than toward staying indefinitely.

## How do you know if you have a revenue leadership gap or a different problem?

This is the question that saves founders the most money, because a fractional CRO cannot fix a problem that lives upstream of go-to-market. Run a quick differential diagnosis. If prospects take meetings, express interest, and then stall in procurement or ghost after a pilot, that is usually a sales-motion and revenue-leadership gap — a CRO can help. If prospects will not take the meeting at all, or churn quickly after buying, the problem is more likely product, positioning, or a market that is not ready — and no revenue leader will paper over that.

Look at the pattern of your losses. Losing to "no decision" and stalled internal buy-in points to a motion problem: weak multi-threading, no compelling event, no ROI case — all squarely in a fractional CRO's wheelhouse. Losing consistently to a specific competitor on capability, or watching customers leave within 90 days, points to product or fit problems that leadership cannot out-sell. The honest founder audits churn and win/loss before hiring: if net revenue retention is healthy and the only broken thing is new-logo acquisition, you have a leadership and motion gap that fractional revenue leadership is built for. If retention itself is leaking, fix the bucket before you hire someone to pour more in. A fractional CRO can help you build the [win loss analysis](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11412) that answers this — but you should have at least a rough read before you spend the retainer.

There is a simple gut-check that cuts through most of the ambiguity: put your founder in front of ten well-qualified prospects and watch the conversion rate. If the founder — the person who knows the product and the mission better than anyone — can close a respectable share of those deals, then the raw material for a repeatable motion exists and the job is to systematize and delegate it, which is exactly what a fractional CRO does. If even the founder cannot get those deals across the line, no amount of revenue leadership will manufacture demand that the market is not offering, and you are looking at a product, pricing, or positioning problem wearing a sales costume. The discipline of running that test honestly, and being willing to hear the uncomfortable answer, is worth more than any hire — because it tells you whether you are about to spend a retainer solving your actual problem or merely decorating it.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant diagnoses and advises, then leaves you a plan to execute. A fractional CRO operates inside the business, owns a revenue number, coaches your team, and runs the motion week to week. Consultants recommend; fractional CROs are accountable for results.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run 6 to 18 months. The goal is to install a repeatable motion and RevOps spine, then hand off to a full-time hire. If you still need them to close deals after 18 months, the engagement failed to build a self-sustaining system.

### Can a fractional CRO work with a pre-revenue proptech startup?
Rarely worth it. Pre-revenue companies need founder-led selling to find product-market fit, not a systematizer. Bring in a fractional CRO once you have early repeatable signal — a handful of similar closed deals — so there is a motion to scale.

### Should a fractional CRO get equity in my proptech company?
Often yes, in modest amounts, to align incentives with revenue outcomes rather than billable days. Equity or a success bonus tied to pipeline and closed ARR is common. Keep it proportional to a part-time commitment, not a full-time executive grant.

### Will a fractional CRO manage my existing sales reps?
Yes — coaching and leveling up your current team is core to the role. A good one runs your pipeline reviews, fixes your comp plan, and either develops your reps or helps you replace the ones who cannot hit the rebuilt motion.

## FAQ

**How many days a week does a fractional CRO typically work?**
Usually two to four days per week, structured as a monthly retainer. The exact commitment scales with your stage and budget — earlier companies with a narrower scope often start at two days and expand as the engagement proves out.

**Is a fractional CRO the same as an interim CRO?**
No. An interim CRO is a temporary full-time placeholder filling a vacancy until you hire permanently. A fractional CRO is a deliberately part-time, ongoing arrangement for companies that do not yet need — or cannot yet afford — a full-time revenue executive.

**What size proptech company is the sweet spot for a fractional CRO?**
Roughly 1 to 15 million dollars in ARR. Below that you usually need founder-led selling to find fit; above it you can typically justify a full-time CRO. The fractional model shines precisely in that in-between band.

**What should I measure to know if the engagement is working?**
Set 90 and 180 day scorecards before signing: pipeline created, stage conversion rates, forecast accuracy, and a leading indicator like qualified meetings from your target ICP. If those metrics have not moved by the second quarter, re-scope or reconsider.

**Can one fractional CRO serve multiple companies at once?**
Yes, and most do. That is how the economics work — they spread senior expertise across several clients. Confirm their portfolio does not include a direct competitor and that their committed days match what your stage actually needs.

**Do I still need a RevOps hire if I have a fractional CRO?**
Eventually, yes. The fractional CRO designs and stands up the revenue operations spine, but sustaining CRM hygiene, reporting, and enablement long-term usually warrants a dedicated RevOps person or team once volume grows. The CRO builds the system; RevOps maintains it.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a fractional VP of Sales?**
The CRO owns the entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and pricing — and works at the strategy-and-systems level. A fractional VP of Sales focuses more narrowly on running and scaling the sales team itself against an existing motion.

**What is the biggest risk in hiring a fractional CRO?**
Hiring one to solve a problem that is really product, pricing, or market-fit. No revenue leader can out-sell a broken product or a market that is not ready. Diagnose the root cause first so you do not spend a retainer masking an upstream problem.

**How do I evaluate a fractional CRO's proptech domain expertise?**
Ask for specific deals they have closed in real estate or an adjacent vertical, the metrics they sold on, and the stakeholders they multi-threaded. Generalists who cannot name occupancy, NOI, or leasing velocity as buyer currencies are a red flag in this space.

**Should I use a fractional CRO agency or an independent operator?**
Both work. Agencies offer bench depth and process; independents offer direct accountability and often lower cost. What matters more is the individual's proptech track record and whether their committed days and incentives genuinely align with your outcomes.
